summary: Defines MIB objects for managing printers, covering both the physical device and the printing process. It is on the standards track. It has been replaced by RFC 3805.

eli5.summary: A list of gauges so a computer can ask a printer if it is out of paper or jammed.

questions: how do you monitor printers with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and controlling printers remotely.

tldr.problem: Printers are complex devices with many sub-units, supplies, and possible failures. Network administrators need a standard way to query status, detect problems, and manage them remotely.
tldr.mechanism: The Printer MIB defines SNMP objects organized into groups representing the printer's physical and logical components: inputs, outputs, markers (print engines), media paths, interpreters, and alerts. Each group exposes status, configuration, and alerting information.
tldr.outcome: Network management applications can monitor printer health, detect when supplies run low or when a jam occurs, and receive alerts. This RFC was superseded by RFC 3805, which expanded the objects. The MIB framework remains the foundation for printer management today.

today: RFC 1759 was superseded by RFC 3805 in 2004, which extended the model with additional objects and clarified ambiguities. The printer MIB model remains the standard way to manage printers via SNMP in enterprise environments. Modern printers implement this MIB (or its successor) to allow remote monitoring and control.

sections.title: Managing Printers Over the Network
sections.content:
A printer is not just a device that receives print jobs. It is a complex machine with paper trays (inputs), output bins, toner or ink supplies, mechanical parts that can jam, and a built-in computer (the system controller). An administrator needs to know when paper is low, when a cover is open, when toner is empty, or when a jam has occurred. Instead of walking to each printer to check its panel, the Printer MIB lets network management software ask the printer these questions over SNMP.

The RFC defines three categories of information: descriptions (static configuration and capabilities), status (current operating state), and alerts (reportable events like errors or supply shortages).
sections.eli5: Instead of going to the printer to check if it is OK, you can ask it questions over the network and it tells you everything.

sections.title: The Printer Model: Physical and Logical Sub-Units
sections.content:
Rather than treating a printer as a single black box, the MIB models it as 13 types of sub-units. The model flows through three paths: (1) print data comes in through an Interface and flows through a Channel to an Interpreter, (2) media is loaded from Inputs, flows through a Media Path where a Marker applies marks, and exits through Outputs (with optional Finishers), and (3) auxiliary sub-units (General Printer, Localization, Console, System Controller, and Alerts) support and monitor the overall operation.

Each sub-unit is represented by a group of MIB objects. Some sub-units are physical mechanisms (inputs, outputs, markers). Others are logical processes (interpreters for PostScript or PCL, channels for TCP or serial connections). A single printer can have multiple instances of most sub-units.
sections.eli5: A printer is built from building blocks: trays that feed paper, printers that mark it, bins that catch it, and controllers that glue it together. Each block reports its own status.

sections.title: Key Groups and Objects
sections.content:
The General Printer Group reports the overall status of the printer (running, warning, or down) and identifies the manufacturer, model, and serial number. The Input Group describes paper trays: how many sheets remain, what size and type of media is loaded, and whether a tray is removable. The Output Group tracks output bins and their capacity. The Marker Group reports on the print engine(s), resolution, and marking technology (laser, inkjet, thermal, etc.).

The Marker Supplies Group tracks consumables like toner and developer. The Media Path Group describes how media moves through the printer (simplex vs. duplex, buffered or not). The Interpreter Group lists which page description languages the printer supports (PostScript, PCL, etc.). The Console Group gives remote access to the printer's operator panel. Finally, the Alerts Group maintains a table of recent errors and their severity.
sections.eli5: Each group is like a gauge on the printer panel: one for paper left, one for toner, one for errors, and so on. You can read all of them from your desk.

sections.title: Status and Alert Categories
sections.content:
The printer status is conveyed through objects from the Host MIB: hrDeviceStatus (unknown, running, warning, testing, down) and hrPrinterStatus (other, unknown, idle, printing, warmup). Together these map to states like Normal, Busy, Non-Critical Alert Active (e.g., low paper), Critical Alert Active (e.g., jam), Offline, and Standby.

Alerts are split into two types. Critical alerts stop printing: out of paper, toner empty, cover open, jam. The system immediately sends a trap to notify the administrator. Non-critical alerts warn of impending problems: paper low, toner low, output bin nearly full. These do not stop printing but may require action soon. The Alert Table stores alert information including code, severity, description, and the sub-unit affected.
sections.eli5: The printer can tell you it is fine, busy, has a small warning, or is completely broken. It also has a log of recent problems so you can see what went wrong.

sections.title: Object Organization and Read-Write Access
sections.content:
Most MIB objects are read-only so that a management application can observe the printer's state without accidentally changing it. A few objects are read-write: a configurator can set the printer's name and contact information, enable or disable specific inputs and outputs, or reset the printer. The MIB uses standard ASN.1 syntax with defined textual conventions for enumerations (e.g., media type as a number that translates to a name).

Objects are organized in tables (indexed by entry numbers) for lists of similar items—e.g., one row per input, one row per output. Counters track total sheets printed, total pages, and supply consumption. The MIB also references objects from the Host Resources MIB (RFC 1514) for processor and memory information on the system controller.
sections.eli5: The printer data is organized like a spreadsheet: rows for each tray, column for capacity, column for current level. You can read most of it, and change a few important things like the printer's name.

sections.title: Scope and Deployment
sections.content:
The MIB covers management of the physical printer device but does not include job queue management, print job status, or user accounting—those are outside the scope. It focuses on device configuration, status, and health. Implementers must guard against unauthorized changes to read-write objects using SNMP authentication and access control. The RFC assumes the printer runs an SNMP agent software alongside its printing software on the system controller.

RFC 1759 was published in March 1995 and classified as a Proposed Standard. It was superseded by RFC 3805 in 2004, which added many new objects and clarified others. The core model and most of the original groups remain in use today in modern printer management systems.
sections.eli5: This standard covers what the printer can tell you about itself, not who can print what jobs. Make sure only trusted people can change the printer's settings over the network.
